title: Learning Where to Steer: Noise-Space Geometry for Efficient Offline Multi-Objective Optimization with Generative Models

paper.title: Learning Where to Steer: Noise-Space Geometry for Efficient Offline Multi-Objective Optimization with Generative Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Offline multi-objective optimization (MOO) seeks solutions with better objective trade-offs using only a fixed dataset, without querying the objectives. Diffusion models trained on such data have emerged as a promising approach, but their samples are not inherently better than the data and must be steered toward the Pareto front. Existing methods guide or condition every sampling step. We instead act on the initial noise and leave the sampling process unchanged. Across Off-MOO-Bench, we observe that the objectives, as functions of the noise, are sensitive to only a few directions. We estimate these directions once per task via a Recursive Feature Machine using function values alone, and a small cache serves every trade-off, so each candidate costs one noise displacement and one ODE solve. We prove that this displacement increases the learned scalarized objective in expectation, and that sweeping trade-offs recovers the flow’s attainable front up to proxy and steering errors. With additional guidance, for which we introduce novel data-adaptive and Pareto-aware operators, our method attains the best average hypervolume rank among generative methods on 47 tasks, at comparable or lower sampling cost. Steering alone outranks the best prior generative method at a fraction of its sampling cost.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In offline multi-objective optimization (MOO), we are usually given a fixed dataset 𝒟 = { ( 𝒙 i , 𝒚 i ) } i = 1 N {\mathcal{D}}=\{({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{y}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} consisting of candidate solutions X = { 𝒙 i } i = 1 N ⊂ ℝ D X=\{{\bm{x}}_{i}\}^{N}_{i=1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} and their values on m m objectives 𝒚 i = 𝒇 ⁡ ( 𝒙 i ) ∈ ℝ m {\bm{y}}_{i}={\bm{f}}({\bm{x}}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} . The goal is to propose new solutions that approximate the Pareto front without querying the true objectives on new data points. Generative modeling has recently emerged as a promising approach to this problem. In particular, a flow or diffusion model trained on 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} can generate new solutions that lie within the support of the input data X X . However, faithfully modeling the observed data distribution is not sufficient for optimization, because samples drawn from the learned distribution are not inherently biased toward solutions with better objective values than those already present in the dataset. Improving upon the observed Pareto front may require generating out-of-distribution (OOD) solutions beyond the regions covered by the input data X X . Thus, the generative process must be explicitly steered toward high-quality regions of the solution space and, in particular, toward the Pareto front. Figure 1 : The noise-space objective is low rank. (a) Spectrum of 𝑴 𝒘 {\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} on IN-1K/MOP8. A handful of directions carry nearly all the sensitivity. (b) Displacing along them raises the true score. A trailing or random direction of equal norm does not. Existing approaches such as ParetoFlow [ 41 ] and PGD-MOO [ 2 ] achieve this by guiding the sampling trajectory of a flow or diffusion model using proxy-objective gradients or a learned dominance classifier. Such methods require an additional correction or guidance term applied at each integration step during the inference trajectory, increasing inference cost. Moreover, guidance is often constructed from a denoised estimate of the final sample, and this estimate can be unreliable during the early, highly noisy portion of the trajectory. An alternative approach, PCD [ 25 ] , which achieves best prior generative performance, directly trains an objective-conditioned diffusion model and uses classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 13 ] at inference time to bias generation toward desirable objective values. This approach avoids the need for an external proxy model, but places a greater burden on the conditional generative model, which must learn a sufficiently accurate relationship between objective values and designs, including in the high-performing regions that are typically sparsely represented in the offline dataset. PCD also reports diminishing returns as the conditioning strength is increased.

sections.heading: Our work.
sections.text: In this paper, we propose Active-Subspace Noise Steering (ASNS), a novel and lightweight noise-space steering strategy for any ODE-sampled diffusion model. To illustrate the key idea, consider a flow matching model. Recall that the design space of the MOO problem is ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} and the m m objectives are 𝒇 : ℝ D → ℝ m {\bm{f}}:\mathbb{R}^{D}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} . At inference time, sampling begins from a noise vector 𝒛 ∈ ℝ D {\bm{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and follows the ODE trajectory of the learned flow to produce a clean sample 𝒙 ∈ ℝ D {\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} , a new candidate solution. Since the flow dynamics are deterministic, the entire sampling procedure induces a deterministic map Φ θ : ℝ D → ℝ D \Phi_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{D}\to\mathbb{R}^{D} , where θ \theta denotes the parameters of the learned flow model. Thus, properties of the final solution are already encoded through its dependence on the initial noise. This motivates our central question: Can we steer the initial noise efficiently and effectively toward regions that generate solutions near the Pareto front of the MOO problem? Interestingly, we find that such noise-space steering can be highly effective. Consider a scalarization of the multi-objective function, h 𝒘 ​ ( 𝒙 ) := 𝒘 ⊤ ​ 𝒇 ​ ( 𝒙 ) h_{\bm{w}}({\bm{x}}):={\bm{w}}^{\top}{\bm{f}}({\bm{x}}) (in practice with learned proxies 𝒇 ^ \hat{\bm{f}} ), parameterized by a trade-off vector 𝒘 ∈ Δ m − 1 {\bm{w}}\in\Delta^{m-1} . Through the learned generative map Φ θ \Phi_{\theta} , this induces a scalar-valued function directly on noise space, H 𝒘 ​ ( 𝒛 ) := h 𝒘 ​ ( Φ θ ​ ( 𝒛 ) ) H_{\bm{w}}({\bm{z}}):=h_{\bm{w}}\!\left(\Phi_{\theta}({\bm{z}})\right) . Our key empirical observation is that H 𝒘 H_{\bm{w}} is often sensitive to only a few directions in the high-dimensional noise space ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} . In particular, the average pullback metric 𝑴 𝒘 {\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} induced by H 𝒘 H_{\bm{w}} is approximately low-rank across nearly all datasets we consider (see Section 3.1 ) for details and Figure 1 a for an example on IN-1K/MOP8 dataset. This suggests that, although the noise space may be high-dimensional, the objective-relevant variation is concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. If these important directions can be identified, we can steer the initial noise along them so that the resulting samples move toward the Pareto front. To identify these objective-relevant directions, we build on the Average Gradient Outer Product (AGOP) and Recursive Feature Machines (RFM) framework of Radhakrishnan et al. [23] , which can extract task-dependent directions effectively using a few examples. RFM+AGOP has previously been used for activation steering in LLMs [ 4 ] and for steering the activations of image diffusion models [ 33 ] . Our setting, however, introduces an important additional challenge: rather than steering with respect to a single target function, we must handle an entire family of scalarized objectives H 𝒘 H_{\bm{w}} , parameterized by the trade-off vector 𝒘 {\bm{w}} . In Section 3.2 , we show that this family possesses additional structure that allows us to precompute and cache only a small collection of matrices that suffices to support arbitrary trade-offs 𝒘 ∈ ℝ m {\bm{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} . At inference time, given a desired trade-off vector 𝒘 {\bm{w}} , we efficiently construct the corresponding steering directions from these cached matrices and perturb the initial noise along these directions. The resulting “improved” noise vectors are then passed through the original flow model without further modification , producing candidate solutions that are biased toward better objective values and closer to the unknown Pareto front. In Section 3.3 , we provide theoretical justification for this noise-space steering principle, showing conditions under which moving along the identified objective-relevant directions provably increases the scalarized proxy objective in expectation. Our noise-space steering strategy is also modular, since it acts only on the initial noise, and can be applied to any pretrained diffusion model, with or without inference-time guidance. In Section 4 , we develop complementary guidance operators for flow and diffusion models, which further improve performance when combined with noise steering. We summarize our contributions as follows. • We introduce ASNS, a novel offline MOO approach that steers only the initial noise, leaving the sampler unmodified. The directions are the leading eigenvectors of the AGOP of the noise-space objective, estimated once per task with an RFM, for every trade-off (Section 3 ). • We prove that these directions capture the most squared gradient of any subspace of their dimension, that steering along them increases the learned scalarized objective in expectation, and that sweeping trade-offs approaches the best front the flow can generate, up to estimation and steering errors (Section 3.3 ). • Where a single displacement cannot reach, we introduce two families of guidance operators that use information prior guidance discards and never differentiate through the ODE solve. Data-adaptive operators restrict the objective gradient to the learned geometry and the local data manifold, and Pareto-aware operators combine the per-objective gradients, not their scalarized sum, into a direction along which no objective decreases to first order (Section 4 ). • Across 47 tasks and 14 strong baselines, steering with our guidance operators attains the best average hypervolume rank among generative methods and steering alone outranks the best prior generative method at up to an order of magnitude lower sampling cost. Ablations isolate the chosen directions, rank, weighting, and steering strength (Section 5 , § B ).

sections.heading: More related work.
sections.text: Surrogate-based methods fit proxies on 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} and search them with NSGA-II [ 36 , 10 ] , often regularized against exploitation away from the data [ 29 , 37 , 22 , 40 , 6 ] . Beyond the generative methods above, earlier work models 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} for single-objective design [ 18 , 17 ] , SPREAD guides with a common-descent direction [ 15 ] , and a recent diagnosis finds generative methods more conservative than evolutionary search when the data lie far from the front [ 14 ] . Diffusion noise has also been optimized per sample and per reward [ 32 , 12 , 42 , 21 ] or edited along a few patch-PCA components [ 34 ] , whereas we learn objective-sensitive directions once and share them across noise vectors and trade-offs.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We compare three families of methods, separated by rules in Table 1 . DNN-based methods fit surrogates on 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} and optimize them with NSGA-II [ 10 ] . The surrogate is End-to-End (E2E), Multi-Head (MH), or Multiple Models (MM). E2E and MH are optionally trained with GradNorm or PcGrad, and MM is optionally regularized per objective with RoMA, IOM, ICT, or Tri-Mentoring [ 7 , 38 , 37 , 22 , 40 , 6 ] . Generative methods are our primary comparison, since they share our modeling assumption and differ only in where the optimization signal enters. ParetoFlow and ParetoFlow+ guide the flow velocity with a weighted proxy gradient [ 41 ] , where ParetoFlow+ is obtained by replacing ParetoFlow’s flow network and proxy predictor with those used in our RFM variants for a fair comparison. PCD [ 25 ] conditions a diffusion model on extrapolated targets under classifier-free guidance (CFG). PGD-MOO is excluded (§ A.6 ). Ours comprises RFM-AN , our active-subspace noise steering (ASNS) Eq. ( 10 ) followed by one unmodified ODE solve, and three variants that add a guidance operator 𝒢 𝒘 {\mathcal{G}}_{\bm{w}} (Algorithm 1 , line 13 ): the data-adaptive RFM-APG (active-subspace projected ascent) and RFM-DAMG (manifold-constrained ascent), and the Pareto-aware RFM-Cone . None of them differentiates through the ODE solve. All four share a rectified-flow backbone trained on the full dataset and one geometry precomputation per task (Table 4 ). Everything other than where the signal enters is held fixed across the proxy-based methods. Surrogates follow the MM configuration of Xue et al. [36] , the weighted-sum scalarization is swept over the same Das–Dennis weights [ 9 ] , and generative methods select the final 256 256 candidates by non-dominated sorting under the proxies [ 41 ] . PCD needs no proxies, so we follow its published configuration. All baselines are rerun from released code on identical hardware, seeds, and evaluation (additional details in Appendix A.6 ). Evaluation. Following Xue et al. [36] , every method returns 256 256 solutions, scored by hypervolume (HV) against each task’s reference point (Table 3 ), which measures optimality and diversity jointly. We report HV of the full set in the main text and of its non-dominated top half in Appendix D.3 . As a reference level, 𝒟 ⁡ ( best ) {\mathcal{D}}(\text{best}) is the HV of the non-dominated subset of 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} , which a method must exceed to generalize past its data. Since HV is not commensurable across tasks, we aggregate by average rank (lower is better). On each task and seed we rank all methods and 𝒟 ⁡ ( best ) {\mathcal{D}}(\text{best}) by HV (1 is best), average the ranks over the tasks of a family, and report mean ± \pm std over 5 5 seeds. Per-task values are in Appendix D.1 .

sections.heading: 5.2 Results
sections.text: Table 1 and 2 support three claims: (i) Noise steering is effective, (ii) additional guidance operator further improves MOO performance, and (iii) our RFM+AGOP approaches are among the cheapest generative methods to sample, and noise steering alone is the fastest of all. Noise steering improves generative backbones. RFM-Cone attains the best overall rank among generative methods and the second best overall (Table 1 ), and every RFM variant outranks 𝒟 ⁡ ( best ) {\mathcal{D}}(\text{best}) overall. ParetoFlow+, which applies ParetoFlow’s per-step guidance to our flow and proxies, isolates the effect of steering, since it differs from RFM-AN only in where the optimization signal enters. RFM-AN improves the overall rank from 13.56 13.56 to 8.93 8.93 , so the gain comes from noise steering rather than the backbone. RFM-AN also outranks PCD, the best prior generative method ( 8.93 8.93 vs. 9.64 9.64 ). With guidance, RFM-Cone outperforms ParetoFlow ⋆ in every task family ( 36 36 of 47 47 tasks) and matches or beats PCD at about a third of its sampling cost. Guidance further improves performance. Each of our guidance operators further improves on RFM-AN in overall rank. The two data-adaptive operators perform similarly, and the Pareto-aware RFM-Cone improves most, with the largest gains on DTLZ and ZDT, where noise-space-only steering (RFM-AN) is weakest. These are synthetic, box-supported families whose fronts lie far outside the data, and surrogate-based search leads there by the widest margin. This is consistent with the regime Theorem 3 isolates, where the best solutions lie beyond one steering step and late correction on the proxies recovers only part of the gap. On the NAS and MORL families, where the data lie on low-dimensional structure, ours outranks every generative baseline or matches it in mean HV. Sampling / inference cost. RFM-AN is the fastest method on every timed task, roughly four times faster than ParetoFlow and an order of magnitude ( 5 × 5\times to 24 × 24\times ) faster than PCD (Table 2 ). On average, RFM-DAMG samples faster than ParetoFlow with a better HV rank, and RFM-Cone trades further cost for the best HV rank among generative methods, so the family spans the accuracy–cost front, and both data-adaptive variants dominate every generative baseline in rank and mean cost. Ablations. Appendix B isolates the remaining components. Displacing along the leading eigenvector raises the true objective while a trailing eigenvector or a random direction of equal norm does not, and the gain saturates at a task-dependent step (§ B.2.1 and Figure 1 b). Under soft weighting the retained rank is insensitive across a wide range, unlike the hard cutoff (§ B.2.2 – B.2.4 ), and the RFM fit is robust (§ B.2.5 ). One precomputation serves Tchebycheff scalarizations with the same front quality as the weighted sum (§ B.2.6 ), and § B.3 studies the guidance strength. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced noise space steering for offline MOO, which learns the geometry of the objectives in the noise space of a rectified flow with a Recursive Feature Machine and displaces the initial noise along a few cached directions, leaving the sampler as trained. One precomputation serves every trade off, each candidate costs one ODE solve, the step provably ascends the scalarized proxy, and two guidance families extend it where a single displacement cannot reach, attaining the best average rank among generative methods, and steering alone samples fastest of all generative approaches. Our main limitations are that all guarantees are on the proxies, surrogate based search remains stronger on box supported tasks whose fronts lie far outside the data, and the method needs a deterministic sampler and a continuous representation of the design space (Appendix A.7 ).

sections.heading: A.1 Benchmark Tasks
sections.text: Each Off-MOO-Bench task supplies a fixed dataset 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} and an oracle 𝒇 {\bm{f}} reserved for evaluation; Table 3 lists the dimension, number of objectives, and dataset size of every task. Synthetic. DTLZ1–7 (three objectives) and ZDT1–4, ZDT6 (two objectives) are continuous functions with D ≤ 30 D\leq 30 and 60,000 60{,}000 offline designs each, and their fronts are known in closed form. Yuan et al. [41] , Shrestha et al. [25] excluded DTLZ2–6 due to an evaluation error in the benchmark that has since been corrected, so we include them. Neural architecture search. C-10/MOP1–9 and IN-1K/MOP1–9 are the NAS benchmarks of Lu et al. [20] with 2 2 to 8 8 objectives. The categorical design space (up to 34 34 variables) is optimized as continuous logits and decoded by argmax before evaluation, so D D is the logit dimension rather than the variable count [ 28 , 36 ] . MORL MO-Hopper and MO-Swimmer are two-objective continuous control problems in which a design is a full policy parameter vector ( D = 10,184 D=10{,}184 and 9,734 9{,}734 ). The data are policies collected during PG-MORL training [ 35 ] , and the oracle is a MuJoCo rollout. Real-world engineering. RE21–25, RE31–37, RE41–42, and RE61 are engineering design problems [ 27 ] with 2 2 to 7 7 variables and 2 2 , 3 3 , 4 4 , or 6 6 objectives. Several have integer variables, and none has a closed-form front. Following Yuan et al. [41] , Shrestha et al. [25] , we exclude the combinatorial tasks (MO-TSP, MO-CVRP, MO-KP), which would require discrete generative models.

For a reference point 𝒓 ∈ ℝ m {\bm{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} the hypervolume indicator is the Lebesgue measure of the region dominated by F F and bounded by 𝒓 {\bm{r}} , HV 𝒓 ​ ( F ) = vol m ​ ( ⋃ 𝒚 ∈ F { 𝒑 ∈ ℝ m ∣ 𝒓 ⪯ 𝒑 ⪯ 𝒚 } ) , \mathrm{HV}_{\bm{r}}(F)=\mathrm{vol}_{m}\Bigl(\,\bigcup_{{\bm{y}}\in F}\bigl\{\,{\bm{p}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\,\mid\,{\bm{r}}\preceq{\bm{p}}\preceq{\bm{y}}\,\bigr\}\Bigr), (12) where ⪯ \preceq is weak dominance under the maximization convention of Section 2 , so 𝒓 {\bm{r}} lies below every attainable objective vector. sections.heading: A.4 Hardware and Compute
sections.text: Each experiment runs on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB VRAM), on a server with 64 physical CPU cores and approximately 1 TiB of RAM, using PyTorch 2.0.1 and CUDA 11.8. No method is distributed across devices. Baselines use their released implementations with the sampling configurations described above. We compare wall-clock sampling times on the same hardware with identical CPU thread limits and an output budget of 256 solutions. For ParetoFlow and PCD, we follow the sampling configurations and hyperparameters reported in their respective papers [ 41 , 25 ] . We report the mean and standard deviation over five seeds, synchronizing GPU computation at the timing boundaries. These measurements exclude model training and oracle evaluation. RFM additionally requires an initial geometry precomputation, performed once per task and trained-model seed and reused across preference weights. This takes 7.4–22.7 seconds on the six timed tasks and is reported separately from sampling time in Table 2 . The full set of experiments, including all seeds, baselines, and ablations, took approximately 550 GPU-hours, of which 300 were spent on baselines and 250 on our method.

sections.heading: A.5 Training Details
sections.text: For each task and seed, we train a rectified-flow model and objective-specific proxy predictors on the offline dataset. All RFM variants share these trained models and differ only in their steering and guidance operators. ParetoFlow+ uses the same flow and proxies while retaining ParetoFlow’s sampling scheme, allowing us to separate the contribution of our method from that of the backbone and predictors. For PCD, we follow the training and sampling procedures described in its paper and released implementation, with the boundary handling described below. We ensure that input normalization is consistent between training and inference and that generated designs are mapped back to the original design space using the corresponding inverse transformation. We correct preprocessing inconsistencies in the baseline pipelines and apply task-specific bound handling where needed. In particular, PCD can generate continuous designs outside the prescribed box constraints, so we clip these designs to the task-specific bounds before evaluation 2 2 2 Shrestha et al. [25] do not explicitly handle this in their code: https://github.com/jatan12/PCD/ . Discrete designs are decoded using the benchmark’s decoding rules.

sections.heading: A.6.1 Validity of the Benchmarks
sections.text: Hypervolume depends on the reference point and objective normalization, so results from different benchmark versions are not always directly comparable. We found that several task-specific nadir values had been revised across Off-MOO-Bench versions [ 36 ] . Our experiments use the nadir configuration retained in our implementation from the May 2025–June 2026 development period. Under this configuration, our 𝒟 ⁡ ( best ) \mathcal{D}(\mathrm{best}) values are generally close to those reported by PGD-MOO [ 2 ] (within +/-2% of other baseline papers). We evaluate our methods and baseline reruns using the same task-specific normalization and reference points. These settings help explain differences from previously published values. Our NSGA-II-based baseline reruns also obtain positive hypervolume on some tasks reported as zero in the PCD paper [ 25 ] . We report the results of these reruns under our common evaluation protocol. Additionally, following Xue et al. [36] , Shrestha et al. [25] , we omit GP-based baselines, which are costly at this data scale and underperform DNN surrogates.

sections.heading: A.7 Limitations
sections.text: Our work has several limitations. Our guarantees hold for the learned proxies, and the recovery bound is relative to the best front the flow can generate, not the true Pareto front. For our proposed approach, the best steering strength is task dependent (Appendix B.2.1 ) and it lags behind surrogate-based methods on tasks whose fronts lie far outside the data. The method also needs a deterministic sampler and a continuous design representation, so we exclude combinatorial tasks. In future work, we plan to choose the steering strength adaptively per task and to combine noise-space steering with surrogate-based search for fronts far from the data. We also plan to extend the approach to discrete generative models.

sections.heading: B.2 Controlled Parameter studies
sections.text: Noise-space steering has seven hyperparameters. Four belong to the precomputation, the RFM fit that recovers the noise-space geometry. These are the sample budget n n , the number of AGOP iterations T T , the bandwidth ℓ \ell , and the ridge λ \lambda . Three belong to the steering step Eq. ( 10 ), namely the retained rank r r , the weighting (hard, or soft with exponent α \alpha ), and the steering strength γ \gamma . The guided variants add the guidance onset t start t_{\mathrm{start}} and the guidance strength κ \kappa , which we study separately in Appendix B.3 . The main results use one configuration for all tasks (Table 4 ), and the sensitivity studies below instead anchor the steering strength and the rank per task (Table 6 ). We vary each of the seven in turn and ask which of them the method is sensitive to, and whether these sensitivities match the theory. The precomputation parameters should matter little. They enter only through the surrogate error, and 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} converges to the metric of the surrogates as n n grows (Proposition 2 ). The steering parameters are where the theory makes predictions. The choice of directions matters (Proposition 1 ), and a displacement helps only up to a task-dependent steering strength (Theorems 1 and 3 ). Five studies follow below, on the steering strength, the rank and weighting, the soft exponent, the RFM fit, step length versus shape and scalarization.

sections.heading: Robustness criterion.
sections.text: Overlapping error bars do not show that a parameter is unimportant, so we use a fixed criterion. A parameter is robust over its tested range if, for every swept value, the seed-paired difference from the anchor has a 95% confidence interval inside ± 0.02 \pm 0.02 normalized HV. Otherwise it is sensitive , and we report where its good range lies.

sections.heading: B.2.1 Steering strength and the reach limit
sections.text: A single noise displacement helps where the front lies beyond the data and hurts where it does not, and the steering strength at which it stops helping is task dependent in the way the theory predicts. Theorem 1 guarantees ascent on the proxy for a small enough γ \gamma , with a gain linear in γ \gamma , and the term ρ ⁡ ( 𝒘 ) \rho({\bm{w}}) of Theorem 3 , the value the steered noise has not yet collected, shrinks as the displacement grows. HV should therefore rise with γ \gamma at first. Beyond some point, two effects take over. The curvature penalty of Theorem 1 grows quadratically, and once the steered noise leaves the region the flow was trained on, the decode becomes less reliable (Remark 4 ). Tasks should therefore fall into three regimes according to where their front lies relative to that region. A front already inside it gains nothing and degrades once the displacement leaves it, a front reached after a moderate displacement rises and saturates, and a front beyond it keeps rising while the flow extrapolates. Setup. We sweep γ ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2.5 , 5 , 7.5 , 10 , 20 } \gamma\in\{0,1,2.5,5,7.5,10,20\} with soft weighting at r = 4 r=4 , all other settings at the anchor. On MO-Hopper we sweep γ ∈ { 0 , 10 , 20 } \gamma\in\{0,10,20\} under two RFM fits, r = 100 r=100 with n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 and r = 300 r=300 with n = 40,000 n=40{,}000 . At γ = 0 \gamma=0 , RFM-AN reduces to unguided decoding while RFM-Cone keeps its late guidance. Since the same γ \gamma moves the noise by different amounts across tasks, Figure 4 also plots HV against the per-coordinate displacement ‖ Δ ​ 𝒛 ‖ 2 / D \|\Delta{\bm{z}}\|_{2}/\sqrt{D} , the quantity in Remark 4 . The dotted line is the offline data. On MO-Hopper, solid and dashed lines are the RFM fits with r = 100 r=100 , n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 and r = 300 r=300 , n = 40,000 n=40{,}000 . Results. All three regimes appear. ZDT4 is in the first. HV is flat up to γ = 2.5 \gamma=2.5 and falls by about 15 % 15\% at γ = 20 \gamma=20 . The NAS tasks are in the second. IN-1K/MOP8 saturates from γ = 2.5 \gamma=2.5 , and C-10/MOP1 peaks near γ = 5 \gamma=5 and declines only at γ = 20 \gamma=20 . sections.heading: B.2.2 Retained rank and hard versus soft weighting
sections.text: The retained rank r r sets how many directions the step moves along, and the weighting sets how far it moves along each. Indicator weights move the full steering strength along every retained direction. Adding a direction the objective barely responds to therefore lengthens the step without raising the objective, so the step leaves the region where the flow and proxies are reliable and HV falls. Soft weights scale each direction by its eigenvalue. A weak direction receives a small weight, so adding it barely changes the step, and HV should not depend on how many directions are kept. Remark 3 makes this precise. The ascent bound for a weighted step is γ ⁡ ⟨ 𝜷 , | 𝒅 ¯ 𝒘 | ⟩ − 1 2 ​ L 𝒘 ​ γ 2 ​ ‖ 𝜷 ‖ 2 2 \gamma\langle\bm{\beta},|\bar{\bm{d}}_{\bm{w}}|\rangle-\tfrac{1}{2}L_{\bm{w}}\gamma^{2}\|\bm{\beta}\|_{2}^{2} . With indicator weights ‖ 𝜷 ‖ 2 2 = r \|\bm{\beta}\|_{2}^{2}=r , so each added direction adds a full unit to the curvature penalty while trailing directions add little to the gain. With soft weights β j = ( λ j / λ 1 ) α \beta_{j}=(\lambda_{j}/\lambda_{1})^{\alpha} the penalty is set by the spectrum, so directions with small λ j \lambda_{j} change neither term. We therefore expect HV to fall with r r past r ∗ r^{\ast} under indicator weights and to stay flat up to the full basis under soft weights. Setup. We sweep r r up to each task’s r max r_{\max} , and up to 300 300 on MO-Hopper with the r = 300 r=300 fit, at γ = γ ∗ \gamma=\gamma^{\ast} and all other settings at the anchor. Three weightings are compared on the same ordered basis. These are soft weights with α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 , indicator weights (the hard mode of Eq. ( 10 )), and geometric weights 1 , 1 2 , 1 4 , … 1,\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{4},\dots within the top r r , a control that decays without using the spectrum. At r = 1 r=1 all three coincide. Figure 5 : Retained rank sweep for RFM-AN (top) and RFM-Cone (bottom) , mean ± \pm s.d. over five seeds. The vertical line marks r ∗ r^{\ast} , the anchor rank of Table 6 , and the horizontal dotted line the offline data. Indicator weights lose HV as r r grows on every task with room to add directions, while soft and geometric weights stay flat. Results. One direction is not enough. On RE36 every weighting scores about half the offline data at r = 1 r=1 , and soft weighting reaches 1.23 × 1.23\times it at r = 3 r=3 . Past r ∗ r^{\ast} the indicator weights lose HV on every task, by about 23 % 23\% on IN-1K/MOP8 and 14 % 14\% on ZDT4. On MO-Hopper they lose 5 % 5\% to 11 % 11\% between r = 4 r=4 and r = 300 r=300 , a drop that stands out from its seed noise for RFM-Cone. Soft weights stay within 0.02 0.02 of their value at r ∗ r^{\ast} up to the full basis on every task. The geometric control is also flat, so any decaying weighting removes the rank sensitivity. The spectrum decides how much is gained beyond that. On RE36 soft weighting beats the geometric control by about 0.16 0.16 , while on the NAS tasks the two lie within 0.03 0.03 . sections.heading: B.2.3 Step length versus shape
sections.text: Indicator weights, the hard mode of Eq. ( 10 ), set β j = 1 \beta_{j}=1 for the top r r directions and β j = 0 \beta_{j}=0 for the rest, so the step moves equally along every retained direction. They can lose HV at high rank for two reasons. Their step is longer than the soft step at the same γ \gamma , and it is spread evenly over all retained directions instead of concentrated on the strong ones. A longer step pays a larger curvature penalty in Theorem 1 , and a step spread over weak directions collects less gain. Rescaling the hard step to the length of the soft step removes the first effect, so any gap that remains is due to the weighting itself. Setup. We rerun the rank sweep of Appendix B.2.2 with both hard modes rescaled at every rank to the soft ‖ Δ ​ 𝒛 ‖ 2 \|\Delta{\bm{z}}\|_{2} , all other settings unchanged. We report the seed-paired difference in normalized HV between soft weighting and each hard mode, with and without this rescaling, as percentages. Figure 6 : Step length versus shape. Paired difference in normalized HV, soft weighting minus each hard mode, for RFM-AN, mean ± \pm s.d. over five seeds. Positive values favor soft weighting, so a higher curve means that hard mode loses more. Solid lines use the original step, dashed lines rescale the hard step to the length of the soft step. Results. Figure 6 plots soft minus hard, so a curve above zero means soft weighting wins. Both reasons appear, on different tasks. On ZDT4 the indicator gap of 14 % 14\% closes to zero once the step is rescaled, so there the indicator mode only steps too far, and the same holds on MO-Hopper. On IN-1K/MOP8 the gap falls from 21 % 21\% but stays at 2 % 2\% to 6 % 6\% for every r ≥ 8 r\geq 8 , and on RE36 the gap of about 10 % 10\% at r = 4 r=4 does not change under rescaling, so on both tasks spreading the step evenly costs HV even at equal length. The spectrum also matters beyond decay. On RE36 soft weighting leads the geometric control by about 17 % 17\% at r = 3 r=3 with and without rescaling. On C-10/MOP1 the geometric control leads by up to 2.6 % 2.6\% with the original step, but soft weighting leads by about 3 % 3\% once the steps are matched, so the geometric edge comes from step length rather than from a better weighting. RFM-Cone shows the same pattern. Recommendation. Soft weighting wins for both reasons. It keeps the step short when weak directions are added, and at equal length it still places the weight where the gradient is, which supports its use as the default throughout.

sections.heading: B.2.4 Soft exponent
sections.text: Following the comparison of hard and soft weighting, we now study the one hyperparameter of soft steering, the soft exponent α \alpha in β j = ( λ j / λ 1 ) α \beta_{j}=(\lambda_{j}/\lambda_{1})^{\alpha} . The exponent sets how many directions the step uses. As α → 0 \alpha\to 0 every weight tends to one and soft weighting becomes the indicator mode, and as α \alpha grows the weight concentrates on the leading direction, which is steering at r = 1 r=1 . Both limits lost HV in Appendix B.2.2 , the first on tasks with many weak directions and the second on tasks where several directions carry the gradient, so HV should peak in between. We count the directions a weighting uses by the participation ratio r eff r_{\mathrm{eff}} of Eq. ( 13 ). Setup. We sweep α ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 1 , 1.5 , 3 } \alpha\in\{0.1,0.3,1,1.5,3\} at r = r ∗ r=r^{\ast} and at r = r max r=r_{\max} , with γ = γ ∗ \gamma=\gamma^{\ast} and all other settings at the anchor. On MO-Hopper we use the fit with r = 300 r=300 . We report gaps in normalized HV as percentages. Figure 7 : Soft exponent. Top, normalized HV against α \alpha at r = r ∗ r=r^{\ast} (solid) and r = r max r=r_{\max} (dashed), mean ± \pm s.d. over five seeds. Bottom, the number of directions the weighting uses, r eff r_{\mathrm{eff}} of Eq. ( 13 ), at r = r max r=r_{\max} . It falls from nearly the full basis at α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 to a single direction at α = 3 \alpha=3 . Results. Both limits fail where predicted. At α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 the step spreads over nearly the full basis, and HV at r = r max r=r_{\max} drops by 12 % 12\% on IN-1K/MOP8, 4 % 4\% on ZDT4, and 2 % 2\% to 3 % 3\% on C-10/MOP1, the loss of the indicator mode in Appendix B.2.2 . At α = 3 \alpha=3 the step collapses onto one direction, and RE36 loses 34 % 34\% to 39 % 39\% , the same collapse r = 1 r=1 produced. In between, α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 is the best exponent or within 0.1 % 0.1\% of it on every task at r ∗ r^{\ast} , and within 3 % 3\% of the best at r max r_{\max} . At r ∗ r^{\ast} , ZDT4 and C-10/MOP1 are flat because r ∗ = 1 r^{\ast}=1 leaves nothing to reweight, and MO-Hopper is flat within its seed noise. RFM-Cone follows RFM-AN throughout. At α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 the step uses only a handful of directions, about 17 17 of 174 174 on IN-1K/MOP8 and 64 64 of 300 300 on MO-Hopper, consistent with the effective ranks of Appendix B.1 . Recommendation. Any α ∈ [ 0.3 , 1 ] \alpha\in[0.3,1] is a good choice, with HV within 3 % 3\% of the best on every task except RE36 at r ∗ r^{\ast} , where α = 1 \alpha=1 loses 5 % 5\% . We use α = 0.3 \alpha=0.3 , the elbow at the flat end of this range. It spreads the step over the most directions that still keep HV near the best, which protects tasks such as RE36 that need several directions. Below 0.3 0.3 the full-basis curves fall toward the loss at α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 as the step spreads over nearly every direction, and toward the sharp end the losses grow to 39 % 39\% . The elbow therefore gives the best worst case, never more than 3 % 3\% below the best on any task.

sections.text: Steering uses the noise-space metric 𝑴 𝒘 {\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} , the AGOP of H 𝒘 H_{\bm{w}} (Section 3.2 ), which we cannot compute directly and replace by its estimate 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} . The RFM builds this estimate from n n decoded noise samples. For each objective it fits a kernel ridge surrogate whose Laplace kernel uses a Mahalanobis metric 𝑴 a {\bm{M}}_{a} , and it alternates the fit with the AGOP update Eq. ( 7 ) for T T iterations. The converged 𝑴 a {\bm{M}}_{a} are the diagonal blocks 𝑪 a ​ a {\bm{C}}_{aa} of 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} in Eq. ( 8 ). The sample budget n n , the iterations T T , the bandwidth ℓ \ell , and the ridge λ \lambda therefore set how well 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} is estimated, not how the step is taken. They enter only through the surrogate error, and 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} converges to the metric of the surrogates as n n grows (Proposition 2 ), so HV should not depend on them over a reasonable range. Normalized HV against the sample budget n n , the AGOP iterations T T , the bandwidth ℓ \ell , and the ridge λ stat \lambda_{\mathrm{stat}} (rows), mean ± \pm s.d. over five seeds. The dotted line is the offline data. On MO-Hopper, solid and dashed lines are the fits with r = 100 r=100 and r = 300 r=300 . Results. Figure 8 shows that HV does not depend on any of the four parameters over the tested range. Across a 4 × 4\times range of n n , a 3 × 3\times range of T T , a 4 × 4\times range of ℓ \ell , and a 100 × 100\times range of λ stat \lambda_{\mathrm{stat}} , HV changes by at most 1.6 % 1.6\% on RE36, ZDT4, C-10/MOP1, and IN-1K/MOP8, and the largest shift is on RE36 at λ stat = 10 − 6 \lambda_{\mathrm{stat}}=10^{-6} . sections.heading: Study 1. Steering ascends under every scalarization.
sections.text: Theorem 1 guarantees ascent for any smooth scalarized objective and never uses linearity in 𝒘 {\bm{w}} . Ascent should therefore hold under all four scalarizations, with the possible exception of Tch and aug-Tch, which are not smooth. The Tchebycheff value follows whichever objective is currently the worst, so its gradient jumps wherever two objectives tie for that role, and at such points the curvature bound of Assumption 1 that the proof of Theorem 1 relies on does not exist. Whether these kinks matter in practice is exactly what the comparison against the smooth softmin-Tch decides. Setup. The matched-norm protocol of Figure 1 b, run once per scalarization at the same 𝒘 {\bm{w}} and the same base noise. The leading arms displace along the top or the softly weighted directions of that scalarization’s 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} , and three controls of equal norm displace along a trailing eigenvector, a random direction, and the sign-flipped leading direction. We read the true scalarized objective of the scalarization that steered, over ‖ Δ ​ 𝒛 ‖ / D ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \|\Delta{\bm{z}}\|/\sqrt{D}\in[0,1] . All four scalarizations take their directions from the same cached precomputation. Figure 9 : Steering ascends under every scalarization. True scalarized objective against step size on ZDT2 (mean ± \pm s.d. over five seeds, same 𝒘 {\bm{w}} and base noise). In every panel the leading arms climb, the controls stay flat, and the reversed arm descends, and all four reach the same HV. Only the soft arm under the non-smooth Tch and aug-Tch becomes unreliable at large steps. Results. All runs use the balanced weight 𝒘 = ( 1 2 , 1 2 ) {\bm{w}}=(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}) , and every scalarization steers with directions taken from the same cached precomputation, with no refit. Steering improves the objective under all four (Figure 9 ). The top-1 arm climbs steadily, while the trailing and random directions produce no systematic gain and the reversed direction makes the objective worse. The four panels have different vertical scales, because each plots its own scalarized value, so we compare the scalarizations through hypervolume, which is the same metric for all four. Irrespective of the scalarization, steering raises the hypervolume by 3.6 % 3.6\% to 4.6 % 4.6\% and all four attain the same level, within one percentage point of one another. The precomputation therefore serves every scalarization equally well, and the ascent of Theorem 1 is not specific to the weighted sum. The one difference concerns smoothness. Theorem 1 guarantees ascent only for a smooth objective (Assumption 1 ). Tch and aug-Tch violate this assumption, because they take a minimum over the objectives and so have a kink wherever the minimizing objective switches. softmin-Tch replaces the minimum with a smooth approximation and satisfies it. The soft arm shows the consequence. Under Tch and aug-Tch it stops improving once the step size ‖ Δ ​ 𝒛 ‖ / D \|\Delta{\bm{z}}\|/\sqrt{D} reaches about 0.5 0.5 , and its results vary much more across runs, with a standard deviation of about 0.24 0.24 at the largest step. Under softmin-Tch it keeps climbing with a standard deviation of 0.05 0.05 . Smoothing the scalarization is therefore enough to restore reliable ascent, as the theorem predicts. The top-1 arm stays consistent under all four scalarizations, including the non-smooth ones.

sections.heading: Study 2: One precomputation serves every scalarization.
sections.text: Study 1 showed that steering works under every scalarization when its directions come from the cached precomputation. This study asks what the cache costs. The cache is fit once, and for any new weight it assembles 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} without refitting and without running the flow. For the weighted sum the assembly is the bilinear combination of Eq. ( 8 ). For the Tchebycheff family, whose gradient is not linear in 𝒘 {\bm{w}} , the same cached per-sample gradients are recombined directly. The most accurate alternative is to refit the RFM from scratch at every weight. We compare the two in quality and in cost. Setup. ZDT2, five runs, seven weights spread across the simplex. At each weight and for each scalarization we build 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} from the cache and from a fresh refit, steer the same starting noise with both, and compare the hypervolume of the results, normalized by that of the best offline designs. For the weighted sum we also refit with the features held fixed to those of the cache, which checks that Eq. ( 8 ) is implemented exactly. Figure 10 : One precomputation serves every scalarization at a fraction of the cost of refitting. (a) HV of cache-based steering minus that of refit-based steering on ZDT2 (mean and 95% CI over five runs, grey band ± 0.02 \pm 0.02 ). The cache matches or beats the refit at the balanced weight and trails it by a few percent elsewhere, similarly for all four scalarizations. (b) Cost per weight on a log scale. The precomputation runs once, a refit takes 0.56 0.56 s per weight, and cache assembly takes about a millisecond. Neither path runs the flow to build 𝑴 ^ 𝒘 \widehat{\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} . (c) Difference between the cache and refit matrices. With features held fixed, the refit reproduces the weighted-sum assembly to about 10 − 4 10^{-4} , so Eq. ( 8 ) is exact. A free refit differs by 6 % 6\% to 24 % 24\% for every scalarization, because it learns new features. Results. Nonlinear scalarizations run from the cache just as the weighted sum does. They need no refit and no flow evaluations, and assembly costs less than 0.2 % 0.2\% of a refit for every scalarization, about a millisecond against 0.56 0.56 s per weight (Figure 10 b). The weighted sum assembles two to three times faster than the Tchebycheff family. sections.text: Algorithm 1 runs in two phases. The one-time precomputation learns the noise-space geometry of the objectives: it draws seeds from the prior, decodes each through the flow, scores the resulting design with the proxies, and fits an RFM surrogate ϕ a \phi_{a} to every objective map g a g_{a} . The surrogate supplies cheap analytic gradients, so we obtain the gradient-covariance blocks 𝑪 a ​ b {\bm{C}}_{ab} without ever differentiating through Φ θ \Phi_{\theta} . These blocks are the only quantities carried forward. The steering phase produces one candidate per weight 𝒘 {\bm{w}} . sections.text: The one thing the metric cannot supply is orientation. 𝑴 𝒘 {\bm{M}}_{\bm{w}} is built from outer products ∇ H 𝒘 ∇ H 𝒘 ⊤ \nabla H_{\bm{w}}\nabla H_{\bm{w}}^{\top} and is invariant to flipping the sign of any eigenvector, so it identifies which directions the objective is sensitive to but not which way along them is uphill. An empirical sign that disagrees with the population sign costs only the share of the gain carried by that direction (Remark 1 ).

If the front contains a flat face orthogonal to 𝒘 {\bm{w}} , every point on that face has the same scalarized value as the maximizer, so the value gap is zero while the distance can be as large as the face. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.38920v1 [cs.LG] 30 Sep 2026 Learning Where to Steer: Noise-Space Geometry for Efficient Offline Multi-Objective Optimization with Generative Models Yuan Lu Esha Singh Yi-An Ma Yusu Wang Affiliation: Halıcıoğlu Data Science Institute, UC San Diego Affiliation: Department of Computer Science & Engineering, UC San Diego Abstract Offline multi-objective optimization (MOO) seeks solutions with better objective trade-offs using only a fixed dataset, without querying the objectives. Diffusion models trained on such data have emerged as a promising approach, but their samples are not inherently better than the data and must be steered toward the Pareto front. Existing methods guide or condition every sampling step. We instead act on the initial noise and leave the sampling process unchanged. Across Off-MOO-Bench, we observe that the objectives, as functions of the noise, are sensitive to only a few directions. We estimate these directions once per task via a Recursive Feature Machine using function values alone, and a small cache serves every trade-off, so each candidate costs one noise displacement and one ODE solve. We prove that this displacement increases the learned scalarized objective in expectation, and that sweeping trade-offs recovers the flow’s attainable front up to proxy and steering errors. With additional guidance, for which we introduce novel data-adaptive and Pareto-aware operators, our method attains the best average hypervolume rank among generative methods on 47 tasks, at comparable or lower sampling cost. Steering alone outranks the best prior generative method at a fraction of its sampling cost. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 Introduction In offline multi-objective optimization (MOO), we are usually given a fixed dataset 𝒟 = { ( 𝒙 i , 𝒚 i ) } i = 1 N {\mathcal{D}}=\{({ m{x}}_{i},{ m{y}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} consisting of candidate solutions X = { 𝒙 i } i = 1 N ⊂ ℝ D X=\{{ m{x}}_{i}\}^{N}_{i=1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} and their values on m m objectives 𝒚 i = 𝒇 ⁡ ( 𝒙 i ) ∈ ℝ m { m{y}}_{i}={ m{f}}({ m{x}}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} . The goal is to propose new solutions that approximate the Pareto front without querying the true objectives on new data points. Generative modeling has recently emerged as a promising approach to this problem. In particular, a flow or diffusion model trained on 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} can generate new solutions that lie within the support of the input data X X . However, faithfully modeling the observed data distribution is not sufficient for optimization, because samples drawn from the learned distribution are not inherently biased toward solutions with better objective values than those already present in the dataset. Improving upon the observed Pareto front may require generating out-of-distribution (OOD) solutions beyond the regions covered by the input data X X . Thus, the generative process must be explicitly steered toward high-quality regions of the solution space and, in particular, toward the Pareto front. Figure 1 : The noise-space objective is low rank. (a) Spectrum of 𝑴 𝒘 { m{M}}_{ m{w}} on IN-1K/MOP8. A handful of directions carry nearly all the sensitivity. (b) Displacing along them raises the true score. A trailing or random direction of equal norm does not. Existing approaches such as ParetoFlow [ 41 ] and PGD-MOO [ 2 ] achieve this by guiding the sampling trajectory of a flow or diffusion model using proxy-objective gradients or a learned dominance classifier. Such methods require an additional correction or guidance term applied at each integration step during the inference trajectory, increasing inference cost. Moreover, guidance is often constructed from a denoised estimate of the final sample, and this estimate can be unreliable during the early, highly noisy portion of the trajectory. An alternative approach, PCD [ 25 ] , which achieves best prior generative performance, directly trains an objective-conditioned diffusion model and uses classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 13 ] at inference time to bias generation toward desirable objective values. This approach avoids the need for an external proxy model, but places a greater burden on the conditional generative model, which must learn a sufficiently accurate relationship between objective values and designs, including in the high-performing regions that are typically sparsely represented in the offline dataset. PCD also reports diminishing returns as the conditioning strength is increased. Our work. In this paper, we propose Active-Subspace Noise Steering (ASNS), a novel and lightweight noise-space steering strategy for any ODE-sampled diffusion model. To illustrate the key idea, consider a flow matching model. Recall that the design space of the MOO problem is ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} and the m m objectives are 𝒇 : ℝ D → ℝ m { m{f}}:\mathbb{R}^{D}	o\mathbb{R}^{m} . At inference time, sampling begins from a noise vector 𝒛 ∈ ℝ D { m{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and follows the ODE trajectory of the learned flow to produce a clean sample 𝒙 ∈ ℝ D { m{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} , a new candidate solution. Since the flow dynamics are deterministic, the entire sampling procedure induces a deterministic map Φ θ : ℝ D → ℝ D \Phi_{	heta}:\mathbb{R}^{D}	o\mathbb{R}^{D} , where θ 	heta denotes the parameters of the learned flow model. Thus, properties of the final solution are already encoded through its dependence on the initial noise. This motivates our central question: Can we steer the initial noise efficiently and effectively toward regions that generate solutions near the Pareto front of the MOO problem? Interestingly, we find that such noise-space steering can be highly effective. Consider a scalarization of the multi-objective function, h 𝒘 ​ ( 𝒙 ) := 𝒘 ⊤ ​ 𝒇 ​ ( 𝒙 ) h_{ m{w}}({ m{x}}):={ m{w}}^{	op}{ m{f}}({ m{x}}) (in practice with learned proxies 𝒇 ^ \hat{ m{f}} ), parameterized by a trade-off vector 𝒘 ∈ Δ m − 1 { m{w}}\in\Delta^{m-1} . Through the learned generative map Φ θ \Phi_{	heta} , this induces a scalar-valued function directly on noise space, H 𝒘 ​ ( 𝒛 ) := h 𝒘 ​ ( Φ θ ​ ( 𝒛 ) ) H_{ m{w}}({ m{z}}):=h_{ m{w}}\!\left(\Phi_{	heta}({ m{z}})ight) . Our key empirical observation is that H 𝒘 H_{ m{w}} is often sensitive to only a few directions in the high-dimensional noise space ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} . In particular, the average pullback metric 𝑴 𝒘 { m{M}}_{ m{w}} induced by H 𝒘 H_{ m{w}} is approximately low-rank across nearly all datasets we consider (see Section 3.1 ) for details and Figure 1 a for an example on IN-1K/MOP8 dataset. This suggests that, although the noise space may be high-dimensional, the objective-relevant variation is concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. If these important directions can be identified, we can steer the initial noise along them so that the resulting samples move toward the Pareto front. To identify these objective-relevant directions, we build on the Average Gradient Outer Product (AGOP) and Recursive Feature Machines (RFM) framework of Radhakrishnan et al. [23] , which can extract task-dependent directions effectively using a few examples. RFM+AGOP has previously been used for activation steering in LLMs [ 4 ] and for steering the activations of image diffusion models [ 33 ] . Our setting, however, introduces an important additional challenge: rather than steering with respect to a single target function, we must handle an entire family of scalarized objectives H 𝒘 H_{ m{w}} , parameterized by the trade-off vector 𝒘 { m{w}} . In Section 3.2 , we show that this family possesses additional structure that allows us to precompute and cache only a small collection of matrices that suffices to support arbitrary trade-offs 𝒘 ∈ ℝ m { m{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} . At inference time, given a desired trade-off vector 𝒘 { m{w}} , we efficiently construct the corresponding steering directions from these cached matrices and perturb the initial noise along these directions. The resulting “improved” noise vectors are then passed through the original flow model without further modification , producing candidate solutions that are biased toward better objective values and closer to the unknown Pareto front. In Section 3.3 , we provide theoretical justification for this noise-space steering principle, showing conditions under which moving along the identified objective-relevant directions provably increases the scalarized proxy objective in expectation. Our noise-space steering strategy is also modular, since it acts only on the initial noise, and can be applied to any pretrained diffusion model, with or without inference-time guidance. In Section 4 , we develop complementary guidance operators for flow and diffusion models, which further improve performance when combined with noise steering. We summarize our contributions as follows. • We introduce ASNS, a novel offline MOO approach that steers only the initial noise, leaving the sampler unmodified. The directions are the leading eigenvectors of the AGOP of the noise-space objective, estimated once per task with an RFM, for every trade-off (Section 3 ). • We prove that these directions capture the most squared gradient of any subspace of their dimension, that steering along them increases the learned scalarized objective in expectation, and that sweeping trade-offs approaches the best front the flow can generate, up to estimation and steering errors (Section 3.3 ). • Where a single displacement cannot reach, we introduce two families of guidance operators that use information prior guidance discards and never differentiate through the ODE solve. Data-adaptive operators restrict the objective gradient to the learned geometry and the local data manifold, and Pareto-aware operators combine the per-objective gradients, not their scalarized sum, into a direction along which no objective decreases to first order (Section 4 ). • Across 47 tasks and 14 strong baselines, steering with our guidance operators attains the best average hypervolume rank among generative methods and steering alone outranks the best prior generative method at up to an order of magnitude lower sampling cost. Ablations isolate the chosen directions, rank, weighting, and steering strength (Section 5 , § B ). More related work. Surrogate-based methods fit proxies on 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} and search them with NSGA-II [ 36 , 10 ] , often regularized against exploitation away from the data [ 29 , 37 , 22 , 40 , 6 ] . Beyond the generative methods above, earlier work models 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} for single-objective design [ 18 , 17 ] , SPREAD guides with a common-descent direction [ 15 ] , and a recent diagnosis finds generative methods more conservative than evolutionary search when the data lie far from the front [ 14 ] . Diffusion noise has also been optimized per sample and per reward [ 32 , 12 , 42 , 21 ] or edited along a few patch-PCA components [ 34 ] , whereas we learn objective-sensitive directions once and share them across noise vectors and trade-offs. 2 Preliminaries Offline multi-objective optimization.
